Locating faults in relay circuits may at first seem complex.
However, tracing input signals from the beginning through each relay to the output makes finding faults easy.
Remember, relays are nothing more than magnetically operated switches.
Relay schematics show the de-energized state.
Let's begin the lesson on TROUBLESHOOTING RELAYS AND SWITCHES...............

The following common relay faults require corrective action to be taken.
Of course, the corrective action for faulted sealed relays is to replace the entire relay.
Let's cover faulted magnetic coils first.
The magnetic core is a soft iron cylinder or ferrite material that has a wire wrapped around it, much like an inductor, this is called the coil. Coil windi)

The coil opens or shorts. In either case coil windings cannot be repaired.
If the coil is open, current does not flow and no magnetic field is produced. The relay will not energize.
If the coil is shorted, current flows but, the strength of the magnetic field is reduced. The relay will not energize.
An ohmmeter check can quickly determine an open or shorted coil.
INFINITY
The resistance of a good coil should measure above 0 ohms and below infinity ohms.
An open coil will measure infinity. A shorted coil will measure 0 ohms.
In most relays, the coil can not be replaced. For an open or shorted coil you must replace the entire relay.
The second common fault is failed contacts.................
A faulted common terminal prevents the relay from passing an input signal when de-energized or energized.
MAIN - OUTPUT
MAIN - NO OUTPUT
A faulted normally closed contact prevents an output when the relay is de-energized. The relay operates correctly when energized.
MAIN - NO OUTPUT
MAIN - OUTPUT
A faulted normally opened contact prevents an output when the relay is energized. The relay operates correctly when de-energized.
MAIN - NO OUTPUT
MAIN - OUTPUT
A voltmeter can quickly determine if the contacts of a relay are faulted.
Measure the input voltage, the set of contacts that are made should also measure the value of the input voltage.
Sometimes, non-sealed relay contacts can be repaired, depending on the type of failure.
Coned and Cratered Contacts - When current flows in one direction through a relay, the contacts may become coned and cratered.
Coned and Cratered Contacts - When current travels in one direction through a relay, the contacts may become coned and cratered.
The crater is formed by the transfer of the metal of one contact to the other. The deposit being in the form of a cone.
Coned and cratered contacts must be replaced. Replace the entire relay if the contacts can not be replaced.
Under normal operating conditions, most relay contacts spark slightly when connected or disconnected.
This causes some minor burning and pitting of the contacts.
Pitting of the contacts actually reduces their size and can prevent current flow from one contact to another.
Burned material on the contacts can be removed (in non-sealed relays) by using a Contact Burnishing Tool.
Other atmospheric contaminates, like dirt, can also be removed by using the contact burnishing tool.
DO NOT use sandpaper or emery cloth to clean contacts in relays. The contacts may be damaged or bent.
Note, some relays use rounded contacts to prevent dust build up and to penetrate any film that collects.
Avoid flattening or otherwise altering the contact's rounded surface with the Burnishing tool.
After using the burnishing tool to smooth the surface of the contact, use a gap tool to adjust contact clearance or gap settings.
Misuse - If too high of a voltage or current is applied to a relay, the relay can fail.
